paper.title: ALERT: Extending Humanoid Motion Trackers with a General and Lightweight Human Avoidance Pipeline
paper.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking has enabled humanoid dancing, athletic motions, and teleoperation, providing a foundation for capability demonstrations and manipulation data collection. However, existing tracking policies lack awareness of nearby humans and proactive avoidance capabilities, while motion substitution and local constraint-based corrections may compromise reference motion integrity and tracking continuity. We propose ALERT, a general lightweight pipeline for extending motion tracking to shared human-robot environments. Through lightweight adaptation, it integrates human perception and proactive avoidance into pretrained tracking policies, balancing avoidance demands with reference motion tracking while preserving existing motion capabilities. Simulation and real-world experiments across tracking backbones demonstrate reliable collision-free execution through localized human avoidance, preserving whole-body coordination and enabling rapid recovery of reference tracking, while retaining the ability of pretrained policies to track unseen motions.

paper.title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
paper.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). paper.title: "I Just Don't Want to Be a Burden": Investigating AI Chatbot Emotional Support Among People with Suicidal Ideation and Other Mental Health Concerns
paper.abstract: People experiencing high-acuity mental health concerns are turning to AI chatbots for emotional support, but little is known about what drives this use, their experiences, and their preferences. We surveyed 202 adults with recent mental health concerns who had used AI for emotional support. Most participants were already receiving clinical care and reported turning to AI, most commonly because they did not want to burden others, rather than being driven by barriers to care. paper.title: Insight into Parametric First-Order Ambisonics Upscaling in Time and Frequency Domains
paper.abstract: First-Order Ambisonics (FOA) offers a practical representation for spatial audio, but its low-order reproduction introduces distinct perceptual limitations during binaural rendering. While recent methods synthesize Higher-Order Ambisonics (HOA) from FOA to overcome these constraints, the importance and potential of early reflections in the upscaling process have not yet been comprehensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap and understand the potential of incorporating early reflections in FOA upscaling, this work develops an experimental framework that selectively upscales these reflections. By utilizing an energy-based criterion, the proposed framework identifies and selectively renders the strongest early reflections with high-order resolution. The selection mechanism is evaluated across three domains: long-term temporal, short-time temporal, and the joint time-frequency (TF) domain. Validation through objective metrics, including the Scale-Invariant Signal-to-Distortion Ratio (SI-SDR), the clarity index ($C_{50}$), and Interaural Cross-Correlation (IACC), alongside listening tests, demonstrates that the TF-domain provides superior performance. By exploiting the sparsity of speech, the TF approach maintains robust performance in complex multi-talker scenarios, providing insights into the benefits of early reflections for the design of future parametric and data-driven FOA upscaling methods.

paper.title: A Unified Choice Model of News Selection: Experimental Evidence on Stance, Rank, and Engagement Cues
paper.abstract: Social media platforms often display visual engagement cues alongside ranked news articles, yet their influence on clicks remains poorly understood when considered jointly with ranking position and users' political preferences. We propose a unified discrete choice framework using a conditional multinomial logit model to jointly estimate and compare the influence of these factors on news selection. We evaluate the model using 1,480 choices from 370 human participants across four news topics in a controlled study with and without visual engagement cues. The framework allows us to assess the incremental contribution of each factor through nested-model likelihood-ratio tests. We find that including visual engagement cues significantly improves model fit across all topics after accounting for rank and stance. Engagement cues alone also predict clicks better than either of these features, although the full model achieves the highest held-out log-likelihood. Finally, we quantify via counterfactual analysis the impact of ranking position and displayed engagement counts on click probabilities. These findings can inform platform owners, researchers, and policymakers evaluating how platform design affects the selection of political news.

paper.title: SPICE: Sparse Parameter Gossip for LLM Pretraining
paper.abstract: Pretraining language models across geographically distributed resources requires communication-efficient methods that operate under limited and variable internet bandwidth. Decentralized training replaces global collectives with peer exchanges, but full-model messages make larger peer neighborhoods costly. We introduce SPICE, which combines sparse parameter gossip with error feedback through corrected parameter values that remain directly interpretable as peer neighborhoods change. These sparse exchanges make broader neighborhoods affordable, achieving better training quality with less communication than the evaluated dense decentralized baselines. As the replica count grows, SPICEincreases the number of peers contacted while keeping individual messages sparse, limiting the quality degradation observed with dense gossip. Under bandwidth constraints, SPICE achieves higher training throughput than DDP and dense gossip, while sustaining throughput during transient link slowdowns.

paper.title: Levio: Smart Actuated Back-Exoskeleton via Retrofit of a Commercial Passive Device
paper.abstract: Passive back exoskeletons show promising benefits for reducing occupational musculoskeletal disorders. However, their assistance cannot be modulated towards the task requirements. Therefore, here, we present an accelerated design pipeline that retrofits a Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) passive back exoskeleton, Laevo Flex, with COTS actuation (CubeMars AK10-9) and sensing (IMUs and load-cell) paradigms. Levio was able to provide assistance based on the user's pose. Nine participants performed stoop lifting with the original Laevo and the retrofit Levio system, in transparent and assisted modes. Compared to Laevo, Levio modulated the assistance provided between the bending and lifting phases of the stoop task. The passive assistance offered by Laevo was $25.2 \pm 4.3$ Nm and $30.6 \pm 9.5$ Nm respectively during the bending and lifting phases of the stoop tasks. Levio reduced the resistive torque during bending to $17.9 \pm 4.6$ Nm and offered increased assistance of $37.7 \pm 6.4$ Nm during lifting. Moreover, participants reported higher usability scores and lowest mean global discomfort score while using the Levio when compared to Laevo. These benefits demonstrates retrofitting passive exoskeletons is a viable direction for rapid prototyping of wearable exoskeletons for lifting.

paper.title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering
paper.abstract: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.

paper.title: The Multivariate Feedback Particle Filter for State-dependent Multiplicative Noises and Its Application to Attitude and Pose Estimations
paper.abstract: Nonlinear filtering with state-dependent multiplicative measurement noise poses a notable challenge for spacecraft attitude determination and robotic pose estimation. This work develops the FPF-DM, a decomposition scheme for feedback particle filters tailored to this family of filtering problems. Extending prior decomposition techniques for additive noise and polynomial measurement models, the proposed method resolves the key difficulty that state-dependent multiplicative noise breaks the polynomial assumption and prevents Hermite spectral backward recursion for the weighted Poisson's equation. By measure transformation and importance reweighting, we incorporate the inverse measurement covariance into particle weights and rescale the feedback gain to restore the polynomial-form Poisson's equation, with the decomposition generalized to non-uniformly weighted mixtures for closed-form gain computation. This general FPF-DM is instantiated on quaternion and dual-quaternion manifolds for attitude tracking and point-cloud registration. Simulations on 4D attitude tracking and 8D point-cloud registration verify that the instantiated filters using only 10 particles achieve superior accuracy and computational performance relative to baseline filters.

paper.title: Plenty to FRET About: From Hazard Analysis to Formal Requirements for Robot-Assisted Dressing
paper.abstract: Understanding requirements for systems involving humans and robots is essential for providing robust evidence that such systems behave correctly. Requirements formalisation approaches such as the Formal Requirements Elicitation Tool (FRET) can support the transition from unstructured natural language to formal representations suitable for verification. In this paper, we formalise 146 hazard-derived natural-language requirements for a Robot-Assisted Dressing (RAD) case study, previously classified using a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements. Through an iterative process involving domain-expert clarification, these were represented by 117 unique FRETISH requirements. Formalisation exposed ambiguities, temporal and probabilistic assumptions, and cases where source requirements needed to be decomposed or could be consolidated because they expressed the same formal behaviour. Temporal analysis showed that 70.1% of the unique FRETISH requirements use either immediate-response or ordering constraints (immediately or before), while formalisation also exposed relationships between requirements across HRT taxonomy categories. We further analyse the formal semantics and realisability of the resulting requirements. The results show that HRT classification and formalisation provide complementary views: the taxonomy captures the teamwork concern represented by a requirement, while FRETISH makes the required behaviour explicit. We report practical lessons and limitations of applying FRET to HRT requirements and identify directions for further work.

paper.title: Where Do Human-to-Robot Transfer Gains Come From?
paper.abstract: Human data can support robot policy pretraining, but gains attributed to a data recipe may also reflect subset size, training variability, or downstream adaptation. In an HPT implementation on a 20-task MetaWorld suite with three training blocks, a constrained random 5,000-recording subset matches most of the task-informed subset's gain over the 40,000-recording pool at 20,000 updates (3.69 of 4.29 percentage points), leaving equal-size selection differences of 0.60 points at 5,000 recordings and 0.45 points at 1,250 recordings, with wide paired intervals. Across 12 comparisons, task orderings repeat across seeds for several contrasts, but a fixed predictor built from the other two seeds trails the mean or difficulty reference in at least one held-out fold for every comparison. Neither mechanism probe shows its predicted positive interaction: task-slot mismatch yields an interaction of $-0.0347$ points after adaptation, and in a six-task observation experiment the observation-by-pretraining interaction changes sign between seeds ($-18.29$ and $+1.04$ points) while full-state pretraining gains are positive in both ($+6.37$ and $+2.31$ points). This retrospective study shows how equal-size and capacity controls, seed-level reporting, and targeted interventions change the interpretation of apparent transfer gains.

paper.title: Low-speed Limit Cycle Walking of Planar X-shaped Bipedal Robot with Special Properties
paper.abstract: This paper proposes a novel planar semicircular-footed X-shaped bipedal robot in which the center of mass of each leg link is at the same position as the hip joint, and discusses a method for generating a stable limit cycle gait on level ground. First, we outline the assumptions of the robot model with four degrees of freedom, and develop the mathematical equations of motion and collision. Second, we set the relative hip-joint angle as a control output and design a control system to follow it to the desired trajectory specified as a fifth-order function of time. Third, we mathematically show that there are special properties: the angular velocity of the swing leg does not change before and after the collision, and the time-integral of the control input becomes zero in a steady gait. We also mathematically show that the model has the feature that approximate linearization is effective and the antigravity effect of semicircular feet can be utilized. Through numerical simulations, we verify the validity of the theoretical results, and analyze some fundamental gait properties such as convergence speed and mechanical energy restoration.

paper.title: Projected Route Cues for Bouldering: Effects of Circular, Linear, and Combined Highlighting on Route Observation and Climbing
paper.abstract: Before attempting a bouldering problem, climbers inspect the route to find its holds and plan their moves, which novices find difficult on walls where many routes overlap. We built a projector-camera system that projects route cues onto the wall and compared three cues: circles on the route holds, limb-colored lines connecting the holds, and both combined. Ninety-six participants, 61 of them first-time climbers, each climbed four routes, one per cue and one without projection, in a Latin-square order. In mixed-effects models, all three cues shortened the time before the first attempt; with circles, its geometric mean fell from 83 s to 39 s. Circles also increased the number of moves made within each trial. Lines led to more use of off-route holds than circles, mainly on routes where such holds lay under the projected lines. Participants preferred the combined cue, although no behavioral advantage of it over circles was detected.
